--- title: "Foundations & Setup" subtitle: "Week 1 · What makes data complex, and how we'll work" author: "DATS 6401 — Visualization of Complex Data · Junjun Yin" format: revealjs --- ## Today's session {.smaller} | | | | |---|---|---| | **Block 1** | Concepts & Theory — *this deck* | ~45 min | | **Block 2** | Guided demo: environment, first chart, first Streamlit app | ~40 min | | ☕ | Break | ~15 min | | **Block 3** | Hands-on: your environment, your chart, your app | ~40 min | | **Block 4** | Wrap-up & homework preview | ~10 min | ::: {.gw-box} **Goal today:** everyone leaves with a working environment, a first chart, and a first running Streamlit app. ::: # What this course is {background-color="#2E6E8E"} ## A course organized by data *modality* Most visualization courses are organized by **chart type**: bar week, scatter week, pie week. This course is organized by **what the data is**: | Weeks | Modality | |---|---| | 3–4 | Tabular & time-series (the "conventional" shapes) | | 6 | Graphs & networks | | 7 | Text | | 8 | Images | | 9–10 | Maps & geographic data | | 11–13 | **Live model output** — client–server ML | ## What makes data "complex"? - **Structure**: relationships (networks), order (time), geometry (maps), pixels (images) — meaning that doesn't fit rows × columns - **Scale**: more rows, columns, nodes, or pixels than the eye can hold - **Liveness**: data that arrives from an API or a model, not a file ::: {.gw-box} The recurring question of this course: **what does this modality's structure demand of the visualization?** A bar chart of a network throws away the network. ::: ## The end of the road (so you know where we're going) By Week 14 you will have built a **client–server ML application**: 1. A trained model served behind a **FastAPI** endpoint 2. A **Streamlit** front-end that sends inputs and **visualizes** live predictions 3. Deployed, reproducible, and defended in class Every week's skills feed that capstone — and your **mid-term** (multi-modality Streamlit app) is the halfway checkpoint. # How we'll work {background-color="#2E6E8E"} ## Notebooks for exploring, apps for delivering - **Jupyter notebooks**: where analysis happens — messy, iterative, yours - **Streamlit apps**: where results live — interactive, shareable, for *others* This split mirrors real data-science practice: you explore in a notebook, you ship an app. From Week 5 onward, homework increasingly means **a running app**, not a rendered document. ## Tidy data: the shape everything assumes ::: {#10d74c77 .cell execution_count=1} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html}
total_bill tip sex smoker day time size
0 16.99 1.01 Female No Sun Dinner 2
1 10.34 1.66 Male No Sun Dinner 3
2 21.01 3.50 Male No Sun Dinner 3
3 23.68 3.31 Male No Sun Dinner 2
4 24.59 3.61 Female No Sun Dinner 4
5 25.29 4.71 Male No Sun Dinner 4
``` ::: ::: One row = one observation. One column = one variable. Every library this semester — pandas, seaborn, altair, plotly — assumes it. ## A first chart, and its anatomy ::: {#71ee4528 .cell execution_count=2} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](week01_foundations_setup_files/figure-revealjs/cell-3-output-1.png){width=757 height=392 fig-align='center'} ::: ::: Figure → axes → marks → labels → title. We name the parts now so we can argue about them all semester. ## Good vs. bad: what are we optimizing? A visualization is **good** when the reader decodes the right conclusion, *quickly* and *accurately*. - Not beauty (though it helps) - Not data density (though it can) - Not effort ::: {.gw-box} **Discussion (3 min):** think of a chart you've seen that *looked* great and told you nothing — what failed? ::: # The toolchain {background-color="#2E6E8E"} ## Your environment this semester ```bash pip install pandas numpy matplotlib seaborn altair plotly streamlit ``` - **Python 3.10+** (Anaconda fine) · JupyterLab or VS Code - **Streamlit** — today you'll run your first app - Weeks 11+: `fastapi`, `uvicorn`, `requests` Setup checklist is in the Week 1 chapter of the course book; we verify everyone's environment in Block 3. ## A Streamlit app is just a script ```python # app.py — run with: streamlit run app.py import streamlit as st import plotly.express as px st.title("My First App") df = px.data.tips() st.dataframe(df) st.scatter_chart(df, x="total_bill", y="tip") ``` Four lines of logic → an interactive web app. (How that works — the re-run model — is Week 5's whole story. Today: just make it run.) ## Discussion {.gw-discussion} **1.** What datasets do you work with (or want to)? Which modality bucket do they fall in? **2.** Think of one tool/dashboard you use that delivers data interactively. What makes it usable — or not? *(5 minutes — then we set up environments.)* ## Coming up next — Block 2 {.smaller} Live, you follow along: 1. Environment sanity check — imports, versions 2. Load a dataset, first chart, anatomy labels 3. The two-line Streamlit app, running **Then Block 3:** your machine, your dataset, your app. **Readings:** Wilke Ch. 1–2 · Streamlit Get Started · Wickham, *Tidy Data* (links in the course book) **Homework preview:** a small Streamlit app — load data, show a preview, one labeled chart, short description.
